04_marg1250: And … went up armed, etc. JEROME. Aquila, who is not contentious, as some think, but painstaking, translating word for word, where the Septuagint put, “And in the fifth generation the children of Israel went up out of the land of Egypt,” translated, “and the children of Israel went up armed out of the land of Egypt”; although for what we said, “armed,” by the ambiguity of the Greek word it can be understood as “equipped” or “furnished,” because of the goods with which they spoiled the Egyptians. But where the Septuagint put “in the fifth generation,” those who have carefully examined the books of the Hebrews report that not “fifth” but “five” is written, so that the sense is, “and five the children of Israel went up out of the land of Egypt”; and because this seemed less understandable, “generation” was added. But Aquila, both in the other places and especially in this one, is said to have translated properly, as all the benches of the synagogues agree.
04_marg1251: “And in the fifth generation the children of Israel went up out of the land,” etc. Does he wish a generation to be counted in a hundred years, and so “in the fifth generation,” because they went out after four hundred and thirty years? Or is this rather to be understood by the generations of men, from Jacob himself, who entered Egypt, to Moses, who went out with the people? For Jacob is found first, Levi second, Caath third, Amram fourth, Moses fifth. And the Latin translator calls progenies those which the Greeks name, which in the Gospel are called “generations,” and they are numbered by the successions of men, not by the number of years. But others count not from Jacob through Levi to Moses, but through the tribe of Juda, which was the royal one; so that from Phares, the son of Juda, who entered Egypt with his father Juda, to Salmon, who as leader in that same tribe of Juda entered the land of promise, there are five generations. For Phares begot Esrom, Esrom begot Aram, Aram begot Aminadab, Aminadab begot Naason, Naason begot Salmon.

04_marg1255: Phihahiroth which is between Magdal, etc. ORIGEN. Let us see what way is commanded to be chosen. “Turning from Othon,” he says, “make your way between Epanleum and Magdal, which is over against Beelsephon,” etc. Epanleum is interpreted “a winding ascent,” Magdal “tower,” Beelsephon “ascent of the watchtower” or “having a watchtower.” You perhaps believed that God would show a level and soft road; but it is an ascent, and winding. For the road by which one makes for the virtues is not downhill; it is climbed narrowly and with difficulty: “For narrow is the gate, and strait is the way that leadeth to life.” So the road on which one goes is a winding ascent, and an ascent of the watchtower, or having a watchtower. The ascent belongs to deeds, the watchtower to faith. So it is shown that both in deeds and in faith there is much difficulty, much labour: for many temptations meet us, many stumbling blocks, when we wish to do the things of God. Then in faith you will find many winding things, very many questions, the objections of heretics, the contradictions of unbelievers: this, then, is the road to be taken by those who follow the Lord. But there is a tower too on this road, of which it is said: “Which of you having a mind to build a tower, doth not first sit down and reckon the charges that are necessary, whether he have wherewithal to finish it?” This, then, is the tower, steep and lofty with these virtues. Seeing this, Pharao says: “These are wandering.” In Pharao’s eyes he who follows God is said to wander, because the road of wisdom is winding, having many difficulties and windings. If you confess one Father invisible, and his one only-begotten Jesus Christ, and one Holy Spirit, this seems winding, difficult and inexplicable to unbelievers. If you say that the God of majesty crucified is the son of man, who came down from heaven, these things seem winding and difficult; he who hears, unless he hears with faith, says that these are wandering. But be fixed in this faith, knowing that God shows you this road of faith, who says: “Moving the camp from Othon, place it between Epanleum and Magdal.”

04_marg1256: That the people was fled, etc. ORIGEN. Fleeing Egypt, you come to the ascent of work and faith, and to the building of the tower; you come to the sea, and the waves of temptations meet you. For “all that will live godly in Christ shall suffer persecution,” because “the life of man upon earth is a temptation.” But if you follow Moses, that is, the law of God, Egypt pursues you. But see what will happen. “The angel of the Lord,” it says, “who went before the camp of Israel, lifted himself and went behind them. And the pillar of the cloud too lifted itself from before them, and stood behind them, and went in between the camp of the Egyptians and of the Israelites.” This pillar of cloud becomes a wall for the people of God; on the Egyptians it lays darkness. It is not the pillar of fire that is moved over to the Egyptians, that they might see the light, but of cloud, that they might remain in darkness, because they loved darkness, not light. So you too, if you withdraw from the Egyptians, if you flee from the power of the demons, see how great helps are prepared for you, provided you remain strong in faith: let not the horsemen and four-horse chariots of the Egyptians terrify you, nor cry out against the law of God, that is, Moses, saying: “As if there were no graves in Egypt, so thou hast brought us out,” and so on.

04_marg1259: Why criest thou to me, etc. GREGORY. It is not our words that make cries in the ears of God, but our desires. For if we ask eternal life with the mouth and do not desire it in the heart, crying we are silent. But if we desire it in the heart, though we are silent with the mouth, being silent we cry. Hence in the desert, when the people clamoured with voices and Moses was silent from the din of words, he is heard though silent, and it is said to him: “Why criest thou to me?” For in desire a secret cry does not reach human ears; it fills the divine ones.
04_marg1260: No voice of Moses is heard, and the Lord says, “Why criest thou to me?” I should like to know how the saints cry to God without a voice: because “God hath sent the Spirit of his Son into our hearts, crying: Abba, Father.” And he adds: “The Spirit himself asketh for us with unspeakable groanings.” And again: “And he that searcheth the hearts knoweth what the Spirit desireth.” So when the Holy Spirit asks, the cry of the saints is heard through silence. Moses is ordered to strike the sea with the rod, so that it may give way as the people of God goes in, and the waters which were feared, made a wall on the right and on the left, not only know no harm but even give protection. The liquid takes on solidity, and the floor of the sea dries up into dust. Understand the goodness of the Creator: if you obey his will, if you follow his law, he compels the elements to serve you against their nature. I have heard it handed down from the elders that a separate division of the waters was made for each tribe, and a way of its own for each. And this is shown from what is said: “Who divided the Red Sea into divisions,” etc.; and elsewhere: “There is Benjamin a youth, in ecstasy of mind. The princes of Juda are their leaders: the princes of Zabulon, the princes of Nephthali”: a proper entry seems to be listed for each tribe. The Apostle says that baptism was completed in Moses, in the cloud and in the sea, so that you who are baptized in Christ, in water and in the Spirit, may know that the Egyptians pursue you and call you back to slavery, that is, the rulers of the world and the spirits of wickedness, whom you served before. But you go down into the water and escape unharmed, and you come up new, washed from the filth of sins, ready to sing a new song. The Egyptians who pursue are sunk in the abyss, even if they seem to ask Jesus not to sink them again into the abyss.
04_marg1261: ORIGEN. 04_marg1266: THE SAME (Origen). “He is glorified” is not enough: for it is one thing to be glorified, another to be gloriously glorified. For when Christ took flesh for us he was glorified, he who came to seek what had perished; yet not gloriously, because he had no beauty nor comeliness. He was glorified when he came to the cross and bore death. Hence: “Father, the hour is come, glorify thy Son,” etc. So the passion of the cross was his glory, where he was glorified, not gloriously indeed, but humbly. Hence: “He humbled himself unto death, even to the death of the cross.” And elsewhere: “Let us condemn him to a most shameful death.” So in these he was glorified, but humbly, not gloriously. Hence: “Ought not Christ to have suffered these things, and so to enter into his glory?” When he comes in the glory of the Father and of the angels to judge the earth, and slays the true Pharao, that is, the devil, with the spirit of his mouth, when he shines in the majesty of the Father: then he will be gloriously glorified, when all shall honour the Son as they honour the Father.

04_marg1268: The horse and the rider, etc. ORIGEN. The men who pursue us are horses, and all who are born in the flesh are figuratively horses, and have their riders. There are some whom the Lord mounts, and they go round the whole earth; of whom it is said: “Thy riding is salvation.” Others the devil and his angels mount. Judas was a horse, and when he had the Lord for his rider, he was of the cavalry of salvation. Sent with the other apostles, he gave health to the sick and healing to the languishing; when he laid himself under the devil, who entered into him after the morsel, he was made Satan’s horse and, led by his reins, rode against the Lord. So all persecutors are neighing horses, but they have evil angels as riders, by whom they are driven, and so they are fierce. If you see your persecutor raging exceedingly, know that he is spurred on by his rider, and so he is savage and ferocious.

04_marg1270: The Lord is as a man of war, etc. ORIGEN. Another text: “The Lord crushes wars; the Lord is his name.” He crushes not only visible battles, but those too that we have against the principalities and powers and the rulers of this darkness. For the Lord is his name, and there is no creature of which he is not Lord. “Pharao’s four-horse chariots and his army he cast into the sea. The chosen riders, the ternistratores, he sank in the Red Sea.” Pharao, as stronger in malice and holding the kingdom of wickedness, drives four-horse chariots: it is not enough for him to mount one horse, but he drives several at once and forces them with the twisted lash. When you see them fouler in luxury, more savage in cruelty, more hideous in avarice, know that they are of Pharao’s four-horse chariots, which he yokes to his car: in them he is carried and flies through the open plains of crimes with the reins let loose. There are other chosen riders, that is, chosen for malice.
04_marg1271: They are sunk to the bottom, etc. ORIGEN. Because such men, that is, were not the stones from which children of Abraham might be raised up, but men who loved the deep and liquid element, that is, the bitter and fleeting pleasure of present things. Hence it is said of them: “They sunk as lead in the mighty waters.” Sinners are heavy, and “iniquity” is read to sit “upon a talent of lead.” Hence the wicked are sunk to the bottom like lead. But the saints walk upon the waters, because they are light and not weighed down by the weight of sin. Christ walked upon the waters, who truly did no sin. Peter walked too, but he doubted a little; for he had something of lead, for which it is said to him: “O thou of little faith, why didst thou doubt?” So all are saved through fire, so that if perhaps anything of the kind of lead has been mixed in, the fire may melt and dissolve it, so that all may be made the best gold, because the gold of that land which the saints are to have is the best; and as the furnace tries gold, so tribulation tries just men. So all must come to the melting pot. For God sits and melts and purifies the sons of Juda. If anyone has brought many good works and a little iniquity, that little is melted and purged as by fire, and the whole remains pure gold. If anyone has brought more lead, more is burnt away, so that it may be melted down more, so that, even if little, yet some purged gold may remain. But he who comes wholly of lead is sunk like lead in the mighty waters.

04_marg1272: AUGUSTINE. Another text: “Thou didst send thy spirit, and the sea covered them,” etc. See, now the Spirit of God is mentioned for the fifth time, so that in this number we may take also what was said: “This is the finger of God.” First, where it is written: “The Spirit of God moved over the waters.” Second, where it is said: “My Spirit shall not remain in these men, because they are flesh.” Third, where Pharao says to Joseph: “Since the Spirit of God is in thee.” Fourth, where: “This is the finger of God.” Fifth, in this canticle: “Thou didst send thy Spirit, and the sea covered them.” And let us note that the Spirit of God is mentioned not only for kindnesses but also for vengeance. Hence above: “By the spirit of thy anger the water was divided.” So the Spirit of God was a spirit of anger to the Egyptians, whom the dividing of the waters harmed, so that as they went in they could be overwhelmed by the returning waters. To the children of Israel, whom the divided water profited, that Spirit was not the anger of God. Hence it is signified that the Spirit of God is named differently because of his different workings and effects, though he is one and the same, who is also taken as the Spirit in the unity of the Trinity. I do not think another is signified, but the same, as the Apostle says: “For you have not received the spirit of bondage again in fear; but you have received the spirit of adoption of sons, whereby we cry: Abba, Father”; because by the same Spirit of God, that is, the finger of God, by which the Law was written on tables of stone, fear was struck into those who did not yet understand grace, so that they might be convicted of their weakness and sins through the Law, and the Law might become their pedagogue, by which they might be led to the glory that is in the faith of Jesus Christ. And of this Spirit of adoption and grace, that is, of this work of the Spirit of God by which grace and regeneration into eternal life is imparted, it is said, “But the spirit quickeneth,” when it had been said above, “The letter killeth,” that is, Scripture that only commands, without the help of grace.

04_marg1273: Who is like to thee, etc. ORIGEN. He does not compare God to the images of the Gentiles, nor to the demons who falsely take to themselves the name of gods, but he speaks of those gods who are called gods by grace and participation in God, according to that: “I have said: You are gods.” And elsewhere: “God hath stood in the congregation of gods.” But these, though they are capable of God and seem to be given this name by grace, none is like him in power or nature. And as to what is said, “We shall be like to him,” this likeness is brought back not to nature but to grace; as a picture is like him whose image is expressed in it as to grace, but far unlike as to substance. For the one is the form of flesh and the comeliness of a living body; the other a coat of colours and wax laid on boards without sense. So none among the gods is like the Lord, that is, invisible, incorporeal, unchangeable, without beginning and end. None is creator of all things but the Father, creating all things through the Son, and sanctifying all things in the Holy Spirit.

It moves me that he says, “Thou stretchedst forth thy right hand, and the earth swallowed them,” as if the cause of their being swallowed by the earth was that he stretched out his right hand. If you consider how the Lord, lifted up on the cross, stretched out his hand all the day to a people not believing but gainsaying, and how the death of iniquity crushed the unbelieving people who cried, “Crucify him, crucify him,” you will find how he stretched out his right hand and the earth swallowed them. 04_marg1276: Nations rose up, and were angry, etc. ORIGEN. “The nations heard and were angry; sorrows took hold on the inhabitants of Philisthiim,” etc. ORIGEN. As to the history, it is certain that none of these nations was present at these wonders: how then were Philisthiim and the Moabites and Edom and the other nations he lists terrified with fear or angry? But spiritually you will find that Philisthiim, that is, “falling by drink,” and Edom, that is, “earthly,” tremble; and their princes run about and are afraid, gripped by sorrows, when they see their kingdoms, which are in hell, broken into by him who went down into the lower parts of the earth to rescue those who were held by death. Hence they fear and tremble, because they have felt the greatness of his arm; hence too the inhabitants of Chanaan, that is, “the changeable” and “the movable,” pined away, when they saw their kingdoms moved and the strong man bound. So let fear and trembling come upon them: the demons tremble and fear the cross of Christ, on which they were triumphed over, and their principalities and powers stripped. So fear and trembling will fall upon them when they see the sign of the cross faithfully fixed in us, and the greatness of the arm which the Lord spread out on the cross, as he says: “I have spread forth my hands all the day to an unbelieving people,” etc. They will not fear you otherwise, nor will trembling at you fall upon them, unless they see in you the cross of Christ, so that you say: “But God forbid that I should glory, save in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ.”

04_marg1282: STRABO. According to Jerome, it is a kind of trumpet having at the top a reed or pipe, through which it gives a sounding note. The chorus, according to the same, is a single skin with two pipes: through one it is blown, through the other it gives sound; so by both the narrow understanding of the old law is pointed to. For how short and small it is is shown from this, that it is carried in a woman’s hand. According to Cassiodorus, the timbrel is a skin stretched between two pieces of wood, by which the mortification of the flesh is pointed to. And the chorus is a multitude singing together; and it is called chorus as if the song of those of one age (coevorum cantus). So because in the chorus all the voices sound equally, charity is signified by it, by which we are all one in Christ. So whoever renders praise to God in jubilation, let him do this in the chorus, that is, in charity, and with the timbrel, that is, in the mortification of the flesh. Hence: “Praise him with timbrel,” etc.

04_marg1284: And they came into Mara, etc. ORIGEN. After the crossing of the Red Sea, after the dances and timbrels, after the hymns of triumph, they come to Mara, that is, bitter water, which the people could not drink: they come into the danger of thirst. But Moses cried to the Lord, and he showed him a tree by which the water was made sweet; and there God set for him justices and judgment; where, that is, there was bitterness, where there was thirst, and, what is heavier, amid an abundance of waters, there was no other place worthier and fitter. Besides, as to his saying, “God showed him a tree, and he cast it into the water, and it was made sweet”: as if God could not make the water sweet without a tree, or Moses did not know the tree. But if the Law is taken according to the letter, it is bitter, and is itself Mara. For what is so bitter as that a boy on the eighth day should receive the wound of circumcision, and tender infancy suffer the hardness of iron? For the cup of the law is bitter, so that the people of God, not that which was baptized in Moses in the cloud and in the sea, but that which was baptized in spirit and water, cannot drink and taste it, nor bear the bitterness of the victims, nor the keeping of the sabbath. But if God shows the tree that is to be cast into this bitterness, the water of the Law is made sweet and drinkable. “Wisdom is a tree of life to them that lay hold on her.” So if the tree of the wisdom of Christ is cast into the law, showing how circumcision, the sabbath, the law of leprosy and the like ought to be understood, the bitterness of the law is turned into the sweetness of spiritual understanding, so that the people can drink it which has left idols and fled to God. If it hears the law teaching about sacrifices, it at once shrinks back and cannot drink. So into this bitterness, that is, the letter of the law, God put justices and testimonies, as if he shut up the treasures of his wisdom and knowledge in a little vessel. Hence: “We have this treasure in earthen vessels.” So that this water may be drunk, God shows the tree that is to be cast into it, so that he who drinks may not die, may not feel the bitterness. So if anyone drinks without the tree of life, that is, without the mystery of the cross, without the faith of Christ, without spiritual understanding, he will die of the bitterness. Hence: “The letter killeth,” that is, the water of Mara, if it is drunk not changed and turned into sweetness.
04_marg1285: And he shewed him a tree, etc. AUGUSTINE. Was there a kind of wood having this power? Or could God, who did so many wonders, do this with any wood? Yet what was said, “he showed him,” seems to signify that it was already such. Unless perhaps the place was one where no wood at all was found, and this itself was of the divine help, that the Lord showed him a tree where there was none, and by the wood made the waters sweet, prefiguring the glory and grace of the cross. But even in such a wood, who is to be praised but the Creator and the Shower?

04_marg1286: There he appointed him, etc. ORIGEN. Why did he add, “After God had set him justices and judgments, there he tried him, saying: If thou wilt hear the voice of the Lord thy God,” etc.? He seems to explain why he gave the justifications and judgments, namely, to try them, whether they would hear the voice of the Lord God and keep his commandments. For as to the former people, what good or perfect thing was commanded to them, murmuring and gainsaying, who a little later, forgetting the wonders of God, turn to idols? So precepts are given in which they may be tried. Hence: “I gave them statutes that were not good, and judgments in which they shall not live.” For tried in the precepts they are not found faithful; so the commandment was found to be unto death for them which was unto life. For the same thing, if kept, begets life; if not kept, death. So to those who do not keep them the commandments are called not good, and such that they shall not live in them. But with the wood of the cross mixed in, turned into sweetness, and understood and kept spiritually, they are commandments of life. “None of the evils that I laid upon Egypt will I bring upon thee.” He seems to say that if anyone knew the commandments he would suffer no sickness, that is, neither fevers nor other pains of the body. But Job, most just and full of all piety, is covered from head to foot with a very grievous ulcer. But the just do not have those sicknesses which the Egyptians have. For Egypt is the world. So to love the world and the things that are in the world is the Egyptian sickness; to observe months, times, to cling to the courses of the stars, to serve the flesh, to give oneself to luxury and to make leisure for delights, is the Egyptian sickness.

04_marg1287: And the children of Israel came into Elim, etc. ORIGEN. The people is not first led into Elim, where there were twelve fountains of water, in which there was nothing bitter, but very great pleasantness from the thickness of the palms. But first it was led to the salt and bitter waters; and when these were sweetened by the wood shown by the Lord, it comes to the fountains. If we follow only the history, it does not much build us up to know to what place they came first, to what second. But first the people is led to the letter of the law, from which, while it stays in its bitterness, it cannot withdraw. So when it has been sweetened by the tree of life and understood spiritually, it passes from the Old Testament to the New, and to the twelve apostolic fountains, where trees of seventy palms are found. For not only the twelve apostles preached the faith of Christ, but also seventy others, through whom the world came to know the palms of Christ’s victory. So it is not enough for the people of God to drink the water of Marath, though sweetened by the tree of life: the Old Testament alone is not enough to drink; one must come to the New, from which one drinks without scruple or difficulty. The Jews even now are at Marath, that is, at the bitter waters. For God has not yet shown them the tree by which they grow sweet, because unless they believe, they will not understand.

04_marg1288: THE FIFTEENTH DAY OF THE MONTH etc. ORIGEN. O ungrateful people, it longs for Egypt. He who sees the Egyptians destroyed, and the flesh of Egypt, who sees the flesh of the Egyptians given to the fishes and to the birds. It murmurs against Moses, nay against God; but the first time it is pardoned, and the second, and perhaps the third. But if they cease not, but persist, hear what follows. It is related in the book of Numbers, and the same Apostle recounts it, saying: Neither do you murmur, as some of them murmured, and perished by the serpents. These things are written for us, upon whom the ends of the world are come. But if we cease not to murmur and complain against God, we shall incur a like peril or example of offence. For when we complain of the inclemency of the sky, the barrenness of the fruits, the scarcity of rains, and of the prosperity of some and the ill fortune of others, we murmur against God. But these things are pardoned the first time; on those who persist they are heavily avenged, because serpents shall be sent among them, that is, they shall be delivered to unclean and poisonous spirits, which with hidden bites feed upon the inmost parts of the heart.
04_marg1289: The sin of the people is made known for the correction of the readers, that it murmured and was ungrateful for the divine benefits, when it received the heavenly manna. In the second month, on the fifteenth day of the month, which is not written without reason. Recall what was said of the laws of the pasch, and you will find that this is the time appointed there for keeping a second pasch by those who were unclean in soul, or busied in business abroad. Those who were not unclean in soul, or were not travelling far off, kept the pasch on the fourteenth day of the first month; but those far abroad and the unclean keep the second pasch at this time, in which also the manna came down from heaven. On the day on which the first pasch is kept, the manna does not come down, but on that of the second. The first pasch is that of the Jewish people; the second, ours. For we were unclean in soul, who worshipped idols; and strangers and far off, who were strangers and foreigners to the testaments of God, etc. But the manna is given from heaven, not on the day on which the first pasch is kept, but on that of the second. For the bread which came down from heaven did not come to those who kept the first solemnity, but to us who have received the second: for Christ our pasch is sacrificed, who, true man, came down as bread from heaven. Let us meanwhile see what is shown to have been done on this day: On the fourteenth day of the second month the people murmured etc.

04_marg1291: BEHOLD I WILL RAIN BREAD FROM HEAVEN FOR YOU etc. ORIGEN. I should wish first to hold discourse on this scripture with the Jews, to whom the words of God were committed, what they think of what he says: Six days you shall gather continually, but on the sixth day double. It appears therefore that the sixth day is named which is set before the sabbath. But the sabbath is the seventh day. I ask therefore on what day the manna began to be given, and I wish our Lord's day to be compared with the sabbath of the Jews. For it appears from Scripture that the manna is first given on the Lord's day, gathered six days continually; on the seventh, which is the sabbath, it ceases. Since therefore God rained manna on the Lord's day, and not on the sabbath, let the Jews understand that even then our Lord's day was preferred to their sabbath, and it was shown that the grace of God would not come down to them from heaven on it, and the heavenly bread, which is the word of God, would not reach them. Whence: The children of Israel shall sit many days without king, without prince, without victim, without sacrifice, without priest. But on our Lord's day the Lord always rains manna, that is, heavenly words, which are joyful to us. Those unhappy ones sigh even for manna, as their fathers did, and do not deserve to receive it: for they cannot eat what is small as coriander seed, and white as hoar frost. For they perceive nothing small, fine and spiritual in the word of God, but all fat and gross. "For the heart of this people is grown gross." The interpretation of this name also sounds this: for manna is interpreted 'What is this?' The very force of the name invites to learning, that when you hear the Law of God read, you may always inquire and say to the teachers: What is this? You therefore, if you wish to eat manna and receive the word of God, know that it is small and very fine, as coriander seed: for it has something of the herb, with which it can nourish and refresh the weak. For he that is weak eateth herbs. It has also something of stiffness, and therefore is like hoar frost; but of whiteness and sweetness very much. What is whiter, more splendid, than divine learning? What sweeter, more pleasant than the words of God, which are above honey and the honeycomb?

04_marg1294: BUT THE SIXTH DAY etc. ORIGEN. On the sixth day let double be gathered for storing, as much as may suffice also for the sabbath. The sixth day is this life in which we now are. In six days God made this world. On this day therefore we ought to lay up as much as may suffice in the future. For if you acquire anything of good work here, if you store up anything of justice, mercy and piety, this will be food to you in the future. For he who here acquires ten talents shall there receive ten cities, and "what things a man shall sow, those also shall he reap." The rich of this world store up those things which in this world, nay with this world, are corrupted; but good things stored up remain until the morrow. But it is written: Those who were unfaithful kept some of the manna, and worms bred out of it and it putrified; but what was laid up for the sabbath day remained whole. And you therefore, if you treasure up for the present life and the love of the world, worms straightway breed, of which it is said: "Their worm dieth not"; these avarice begets, and the blind lust of riches, in those who have money, and seeing their brethren in need, shut up their bowels from them. Whence the Apostle charges the rich not to be highminded, nor to trust in the uncertainty of riches etc.; nor do worms come to be in us from anywhere else than from the manna, that is, the word of God. Whence: If I had not come and spoken to them, they would not have sin etc. If therefore anyone sins after receiving the word of God, the word itself becomes a worm which ever digs at his conscience, and gnaws the secrets of his breast.

04_marg1298: ORIGEN. Morally. We can understand that for each of us it is morning and the beginning of the day, the time when we are first enlightened and kindled to the light of faith. At this time we cannot eat the flesh of the word, that is, we are not yet capable of perfect doctrine; but after long exercises, after much progress, when we are now near the evening, that is, the perfection of faith, then we are made capable of more solid food. Let us therefore make haste to receive the manna, which yields in the mouth a savour according as each wishes. Whence: Be it done to thee according to thy faith. And you therefore, if you receive with all faith and devotion the word of God which is preached in the Church, be it done to you whatever you desire. If you are troubled, it consoles you, saying: A contrite and humbled heart, O God, thou wilt not despise. If you rejoice for the hope to come, it heaps up joys for you, saying: "Be glad in the Lord, and rejoice, ye just." If you are wrathful, it says: Cease from anger, and leave rage. If you are in pains, it heals you, saying: The Lord "healeth all thy diseases." If you are wasted by poverty, it says in consolation: The Lord raiseth up the needy from the earth, and lifteth up the poor out of the dunghill. Yet if anyone receives it faithlessly, and does not eat it but hides it, worms breed out of it. Nor be troubled that the word of God is brought to this, that it should be thought to become a worm. For he himself says: "I am a worm, and no man." For as it is he who becomes to some "for the fall", but to others "for the resurrection", so also it is he who in the manna becomes sweetness of honey to the faithful, a worm to the unfaithful. For he is the word of God, which rebukes the minds of the wicked, and bores into the conscience with the darts of correction. For it is he who becomes fire to those to whom he opens the Scriptures, who say: "Was not our heart burning within us" etc. To others he is fire, with which he burns up the thorns from the bad earth, that is, consumes wicked thoughts in the heart; and therefore for sinners neither does the rebuking worm ever die, nor is the burning fire quenched. But to the just and faithful he remains sweet and pleasant. Whence it is said: "O taste, and see that the Lord is sweet" etc.
04_marg1299: Another text: In the evening you shall eat flesh, and in the morning you shall be filled with bread. Let the Jews say: what consistency is there, that in the evening they should eat flesh without bread, or in the morning bread without relish? What of divine gift, what tempering of heavenly grace is shown in this? This is that in which they can acknowledge God, who eat flesh in the evening without bread, and say that the majesty of God appears. If again bread is eaten without flesh, let them keep these things for themselves, they who, resting content in the quails, think God is acknowledged. But we, for whom at the end, toward the evening of the world, the Word was made flesh, say that God is acknowledged only in that flesh which he took from the Virgin: for this flesh of the Word of God no one has eaten, neither in the morning nor at midday, but toward evening. Whence: Little children, it is the last hour. In the morning, he says, you shall be filled with bread. For us therefore the bread is the Word of God: He is the living bread, which came down from heaven, and giveth life to the world. But that he says this bread is given in the morning, though he was incarnate toward evening, is to be understood thus: that the Lord came toward the evening of the world and near the end, but by his coming, since he is the sun of justice, he restored a new morning for believers; namely a new light of knowledge, in which those are filled with bread who have received his precepts. Nor wonder that the word of God is called both flesh and bread, and is called milk and herbs, and is named diversely according to the measure of believers and the capacity of those who receive it. Or after the resurrection made in the morning, he filled believers with bread, because he granted for the instruction of the Church the books of the Law and the prophets, before unknown, so that he himself is the bread in the Gospel, but the other books of the Law and the prophets or of the histories are called many loaves, with which believers from the gentiles are filled. Whence: They shall go up into the mountain and shall drink wine, they shall be anointed with ointment. So therefore fittingly we receive flesh toward evening and are filled with bread in the morning, because neither could we eat flesh in the morning. For it was not yet the time. Nor at midday: for scarcely do the angels eat flesh at midday, and perhaps the midday time is granted to that order.

04_marg1312: THE CHILDREN OF ISRAEL etc. AUGUSTINE. Another text: And the children of Israel ate manna forty years, until they came to the land which was inhabited. But Scripture signifies in this place, by prolepsis, recording what was done afterward, that the children of Israel ate manna only in the desert. For this is what it says: until the land which was inhabited, that is, which is no longer desert; not that as soon as they came to a habitable land they left off eating manna, but that they did not before. For it is signified that the manna ceased when the Jordan was crossed, where they ate the bread of the land. But having entered the habitable land before they crossed the Jordan, they could eat either manna only, or both foods: for this can be understood, because the manna is not said to have ceased except when the Jordan was crossed. But why in the desert they also desired flesh, when they went out of Egypt with many cattle, is a great question. Unless perhaps it be said that in the desert there were no pastures, and so, the cattle being less fruitful, they spared the cattle, lest, all failing, things needful even for the sacrifices should be lacking; or whatever else can be said whereby the question may be solved. Yet it is more fittingly believed that they did not desire the flesh which they could have from the cattle, but that which was lacking, namely from the waters, which they did not find in the desert. Whence ortygometra was given them, that is, birds which many Latins interpret as quails, though the ortygometra is another kind of bird, though not altogether unlike quails. For God knew what they desired, and with what kind of flesh he would satisfy them.

04_marg1316: ORIGEN. All that will live godly in Christ suffer persecution and are assailed by enemies; and he who makes the journey of this life ought always to be ready and to stand in the camp. Whence: To him that overcometh, I will give of the tree of life, which is in the paradise of my God. He comes therefore to soundness of judgment who orders his words with judgment.

04_marg1317: SO THE PEOPLE WERE THIRSTY etc. ORIGEN. Another text: The people, he says, thirsted for water, and they murmured against Moses. It sufficed to say that it thirsted: what need was there to add water? The addition is not superfluous. There are therefore divers thirsts, and each has his own. They who are good hunger and thirst after justice. Others also say: My soul hath thirsted after thee, O God. But they who are sinners suffer not a thirst of water, nor a famine of bread, but of hearing the word of God. The people therefore thirsted for water, which ought to have thirsted for justice. But God, the instructor of infants, the master of the foolish, corrects faults and amends errors, saying to Moses that he should take the rod, strike the rock, and bring forth waters. For he wishes them now to drink from the rock, and to advance, and to come to the inner mysteries. For they murmured against Moses; therefore the Lord commands that he show them the rock from which they shall drink. For if there is anyone who, reading Moses, murmurs against him, and the law according to the letter displeases him, because in many things it seems not to hold together, Moses shows him the rock which is Christ, that he may drink from it and refresh his thirst. But this rock gives no waters unless struck; but struck, it brings forth fountains. For Christ, struck and slain on the cross, brought forth the fountains of the New Testament. Whence: I will strike the shepherd, and the sheep of the flock shall be dispersed. For had he not been struck, and had not blood and water come out of his side, we should all suffer thirst for the word of God. Whence: "And they drank of the spiritual rock that followed them, and the rock was Christ."

04_marg1325: ORIGEN. Moses, he says, went up not to the top of the mountain, but to the top of the hill. For it was kept for him to go up to the top of the mountain then, when Jesus was to go up, and with him Moses and Elias, and there to be transformed in glory. Now therefore, as not yet glorified by the transformation of Jesus, he does not go up to the top of the mountain, but to the top of the hill. And when Moses lifted up his hands, Israel overcame. Moses lifts up his hands, he does not stretch them out. Jesus, who, exalted on the cross, embraced the whole world, says: I have spread forth my hands to an unbelieving people. To lift up the hands is to lift up one's acts to God, that one may have acts not cast down and lying on the ground, but pleasing to God and raised to heaven. He therefore lifts up his hands who lays up treasure in heaven. For where the treasure is, there is the eye, there the hand. He lifts up his hands who says: "The lifting up of my hands, as evening sacrifice." If therefore our acts be lifted up, Amalec is overcome. Whence: Lift up the hands which hang down, and the feeble knees. If the people keeps the law, Moses lifts up his hands, and the adversary is overcome. If it keeps not the law, Amalec prevails. Since therefore our wrestling is against principalities and powers, against the rulers of the world of this darkness, if you would conquer, lift up your hands, that is, your acts; let your conversation be not on earth, but in heaven. Lift up you also your hands to heaven to God, fulfil the command of the Apostle: "Pray without ceasing"; and then shall be done what is written, that as the calf licketh up the green grass in the fields, so shall this people lick up the people that is upon the earth; where it is brought in that the people of God fought not so much with hand and arms as with voice and tongue, and laid the enemies low by prayer. Lift up therefore your acts, be instant in prayer: this is the fight of the Christian by which he overcomes the enemy. But I think that by this figure two peoples are signified, of whom one, from the gentiles, lifts up the hands of Moses, and raises on high the things he wrote and their understanding, and so conquers. But the other, that is, the Jewish people, does not lift up the hands of Moses from the earth, nor understands anything high or lofty in him, and so is overcome by the adversaries.

04_marg1328: SO THEY TOOK etc. GREGORY. Moses sat on the stone when the law rested in the Church, but it had heavy hands, because it did not bear sinners mercifully, but struck them with severe strictness. Now Aaron is mountain of strength, Hur is interpreted fire. The mountain of strength is Christ, of whom it is said: "In the last days the mountain of the house of the Lord shall be prepared on the top of mountains." But the fire is the Holy Ghost, whom Christ came to send upon the earth. Aaron therefore and Hur, by holding up the heavy hands of Moses, make them lighter, because the mediator of God and men, coming with the fire of the Holy Ghost, showed us the heavy commands of the law (which, while they were held carnally, could not be borne) to be bearable through spiritual understanding. For he made as it were the hands of Moses light who turned the weight of the commands of the law to the truth of confession, according to that: "I desire not the death of the sinner, but that he be converted and live." Hence it is said to the sinful soul: If a man put away his wife, and she go from him, and marry another man, shall he return to her any more? shall not that woman be polluted, and defiled? but thou hast prostituted thyself to many lovers: nevertheless return to me, saith the Lord. Behold, he has given the example of a shameful woman, showing that after shame she cannot be received; but he overcomes the very example by mercy, when he says that the woman who commits fornication cannot be received, and yet waits to receive the soul that commits fornication. Let us weigh the weight of so great a goodness. He says what cannot be done, and shows that he can do this very thing against custom. Behold, he calls even those whom he declares defiled; those he seeks even to embrace, by whom he complains that he has been forsaken. He bent therefore the hardness of the law to mercy, since those whom it justly condemns, he himself mercifully frees.

04_marg1334: AND AARON CAME etc. ORIGEN. Another text: There came, he says, the elders, Aaron, and all Israel, to eat bread with the father in law of Moses in the sight of God. Not all eat bread in the sight of God, but they who are elders, who are ancients, that is, who are perfect and proved by their merits, who, whether they eat or drink, do it to the glory of God. Whatever therefore the saints do, they do in the sight of God: the sinner flees from the sight of God. Adam, after he sinned, fled from the sight of the Lord, and being asked, answered: I heard thy voice, O Lord, and I hid myself, because I was naked. Cain went out from the face of the Lord, because he was unworthy of the sight of the Lord. Moreover, they who receive a fuller knowledge of God, if they do evil, do it before God. Whence: To thee only have I sinned, and have done evil before thee. He who does evil before God straightway repents, and says: I have sinned. He who departs from the sight of God knows not how to be converted and to cleanse his sin by repenting. This therefore is the difference between doing evil before God, and departing from the sight of God.

04_marg1337: TO SHEW THE PRECEPTS etc. It can be asked how Moses said this here, when as yet no law of God had been written; unless because the law of God is everlasting, which all who live piously consult, that what they find in it they may do or command or forbid, according as it has commanded by that unchangeable truth. For must it be believed that Moses, though God spoke with him, was wont to consult the Lord on each point, if there was anything in the disputes of so great a multitude, which held him in the business of judging from morning until evening? And yet unless he consulted the Lord presiding over his mind, and attended to the eternal law, he could not judge justly.
04_marg1338: BUT HEAR MY WORDS etc. AUGUSTINE. The first question is why God suffered his servant, with whom he himself spoke so many and such great things, to be admonished by a foreigner. In which Scripture admonishes us that, through whomsoever the counsel of truth is given, it ought not to be despised. It is to be seen also whether perhaps God willed Moses to be admonished by a foreigner at that point where he could be tempted by pride. He sat in the loftiness of a judge: for Jethro himself indicates this sense, when he bade those be chosen for judging who hated pride. Then, how much what Scripture says elsewhere is to be observed: "My son, meddle not with many matters", appears clearly enough here. The words of Jethro also are to be considered. For he says: Now therefore hear me, I will give thee counsel, and God shall be with thee. Where it seems to me to be signified that the mind too intent on human actions is in a manner emptied of God, with whom it is made the fuller, the more freely it reaches out to things above and eternal.
04_marg1339: BE THOU TO THE PEOPLE etc. THE SAME. But what he adds: Be thou to the people in those things that pertain to God, and thou shalt bring their words to God; and thou shalt testify to them the precepts of God and his law; and thou shalt show them the ways in which they shall walk, and the works which they are to do, shows that these things are to be done with the whole people. For he does not say: Thou shalt bring the words of each one to God, but their words, since he had said above: Be thou to the people in those things that are to God. After these things he admonishes that the business of individuals which they had among themselves be left aside, able men having been chosen, who worship God, just men who hate pride, whom he had appointed over thousands, others over hundreds, others over fifties, others over tens. Thus he removed perilous occupations from Moses. Nor did he burden these, since a thousand had one over them, and under them ten others, and under these twenty, and under these a hundred others, so that scarcely anything that needed to be judged would come to each of those set over them. An example of humility also is suggested, in that Moses, with whom God spoke, did not disdain or despise the counsel of a foreigner; although whether Jethro himself, since he was not an Israelite, is to be counted among the men who worship the one God and are religiously wise, as Job, is rightly asked; nay, it is held the more credible. For the words are set down ambiguously, whether he sacrificed to the true God among his people when he saw his son in law, or whether Moses himself worshipped him; although, as to the worship, if it had been expressly set down, it would seem to be an honour paid to the father in law, as is wont to be shown to men for the sake of honouring them. But whom he calls grammatoysagogas, whom decurions, cannot easily be known, since we have this name in no use, either of offices or of masters. For some have interpreted them teachers of letters, namely those who bring in to letters, as the Greek word sounds. Here certainly it is signified that before the Law was given the Hebrews had letters, but when these began to be I know not whether it can be traced. Thou shalt ordain them, he says, tribunes and centurions etc. And they shall judge the people at every hour; but what is weightier they shall refer to thee. 04_marg1358: AND ALL MOUNT SINAI etc. GREGORY. The Lord, when about to give the Law, came down in fire and smoke, because he enlightens the humble by the brightness of his showing, and darkens the proud by the darkness of error. First therefore the mind is to be cleansed from the desire of temporal glory and from all carnal concupiscence, and then raised to the keen gaze of contemplation. Whence, when the law is received, the people is forbidden to approach the mountain, that, since with a mind still weak it desires earthly things, it may not presume upon the sublime. Whence it is rightly said: "If a beast shall touch the mount, it shall be stoned." For a beast touches the mount when the mind, subject to irrational desires, raises itself to the heights of contemplation; but it is struck with stones, because, not bearing the highest things, it is slain by the blows of the weight from above. They therefore who strive to lay hold of the summit of perfection, when they desire to hold the citadel of contemplation, let them first prove themselves by exercise in the field of work, that they may know carefully whether they now inflict no evils on their neighbours, whether they bear with equanimity those inflicted, whether, when temporal goods are set before it, the mind is not loosed in gladness, and, when they are withdrawn, is not wounded with too great grief; and then let them weigh whether, when they return within to themselves, in searching out spiritual things they do not draw with them the shadows of bodily things, or, if perhaps drawn, drive them away with the hand of discretion; whether, desiring to see the uncircumscribed light, they press down all the images of their own circumscription; and whether, in that which they seek to reach above themselves, they overcome what they are.
04_marg1359: The sacred words, at the beginning of their narratives, express qualities, and the ends of matters; sometimes from the position of a place, sometimes from the position of a body, sometimes from the quality of the air, sometimes from the quality of the time, they signify what they will set down of the action to come. For from the position of places they express the merits of what follows and the ends of matters, as it is said of Israel: That it could not hear the words of God on the mountain, but received the precepts in the plains; indicating the following weakness of the people, which could not go up to the highest things, but slackened itself in the lowest by living negligently. From the position of a body, as in the Acts of the apostles Stephen declares that he saw Jesus, who sits at the right hand of power, standing. For to stand belongs to one who helps, and he is rightly seen to stand who gives aid in the war of the contest. From the quality of the air, as when, at the Lord's preaching, the Evangelist would say that none of Judea would then believe: And it was winter. For it is written: Iniquity shall abound, and the charity of many shall grow cold. He took care therefore to express the time of winter, to show that the cold of malice was in the hearts of the hearers. Of Peter also, when he was about to deny, it is set down first that it was cold, and standing at the fire of coals he warmed himself. For he had already grown torpid from the heat of charity, and, his weakness burning, he warmed himself at the love of the present life, as at the coals of the persecutors. From the quality of the time, as Judas, who was not to return to pardon, is said to have gone out at night to the perfidy of the betrayal, since, as he went out, the evangelist says: "And it was night." And to the wicked rich man it is said: This night do they require thy soul of thee. Solomon also, who was not to persevere, is said to have received wisdom in sleep and in the night. Hence it is that the angels come to Abraham at midday; but when about to punish Sodom they are recorded to have come in the evening.

04_marg1361: ORIGEN. He who despises the present world, namely Egypt, and, translated by the word of God, is not found, because he hastens to the world to come, of him God says: I am the Lord God etc. Not to those only who set out from Egypt, but to those who no longer serve the Egyptians, brought out of Egypt, out of the house of bondage. The business of the world, the acts of the flesh, are the house of bondage; as to leave worldly things and to live according to God is the house of freedom. Whence: If you continue in my word, you shall know the truth, and the truth shall make you free. Egypt therefore is the house of bondage; Judea and Jerusalem, the house of freedom. Whence: "That Jerusalem, which is above, is free." As therefore the earthly Egypt is called the house of bondage for the children of Israel in comparison with Judea and Jerusalem, which is to them the house of freedom: so in comparison with the heavenly Jerusalem, which is the mother of freedom, the whole world and the things that are in it are called the house of bondage; and because from the paradise of freedom we came through sin to the bondage of the world, the first word of the decalogue is of freedom: I am the Lord thy God, who brought thee out of the land of Egypt etc. This voice you will not be able to hear in Egypt, even if it be enjoined you to keep the pasch, to gird your loins, to take sandals on your feet, to hold a staff in your hand, and to eat unleavened bread with bitterness. But neither in the first mansion, nor in the second, nor in the third, nor when you have crossed the Red Sea, even if you have come to Mara and the bitterness has been turned for you into sweetness, nor in Elim, where there were twelve fountains of water and seventy palm trees, even if you have passed Raphidim and gone up by the other stages, are you yet judged fit, but when you have come to mount Sina. Scarcely therefore will you at length deserve to receive the precepts of freedom, and to hear: I am the Lord thy God, who brought thee out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of bondage. Yet this is not a word of command, but shows who it is that commands. The first commandment therefore is: Thou shalt have no other gods but me.
04_marg1362: It is asked how the ten precepts of the law are to be divided. Whether there are four, up to the precept of the sabbath, which pertain to God, and the six remaining, of which the first is: Honour thy father and mother, which pertain to man? Or rather are those three, and these seven? For they who say those are four separate what is said: Thou shalt have no other gods but me, so that another precept is: Thou shalt not make to thyself an idol etc., where images are forbidden to be worshipped. But they will have it one: Thou shalt not covet thy neighbour's wife, Thou shalt not covet thy neighbour's house, and all to the end. But they who say those are three and these seven will have it one, whatever is commanded of worshipping the one God, lest anything else besides him be worshipped for God: and these last are divided into two, so that one is: Thou shalt not covet thy neighbour's wife, another: Thou shalt not covet thy neighbour's house. Yet that the precepts are ten neither party doubts, because Scripture testifies it. But to me it seems more fitting to take those as three and these as seven. Because those which pertain to God seem to suggest the Trinity; and what is said: Thou shalt have no other gods but me, this very thing is more perfectly unfolded when images are forbidden to be worshipped. But the coveting of another's wife and the coveting of another's house differ so much in sinning that to that in which it is said: Thou shalt not covet thy neighbour's house, other things were joined, Scripture saying: nor his field, nor his servant, nor his handmaid, nor his oxen etc. And it seems to have distinguished the coveting of another's wife from the coveting of any other thing of another's, when it began both thus: Thou shalt not covet thy neighbour's wife, Thou shalt not covet thy neighbour's house, and to this joined the rest. But it did not, when it had said: Thou shalt not covet thy neighbour's wife, join other things to this, saying: nor his house, nor his field etc.; but all these appear to be joined, as contained in one precept, and distinguished from that in which the wife is named. But as for that where it is said: Thou shalt have no other gods but me, it is plain that the diligent carrying out of this matter is in the things set down after it. For to what does: Thou shalt not make to thyself an idol, nor any image etc., pertain, but to what is said: Thou shalt have no other gods but me?

04_marg1364: THOU SHALT NOT HAVE STRANGE GODS etc. ORIGEN. The first commandment is: Thou shalt have no other gods but me; and there follows: Thou shalt not make to thyself an idol, nor any likeness etc. Some think all these together are one commandment; and if it be reckoned so, the number of ten commandments will not be filled. The first commandment therefore is: Thou shalt have no other gods but me. The second: Thou shalt not make to thyself an idol, nor any likeness etc. Let us begin therefore from the first commandment: Thou shalt have no other gods but me. Had he said: 'There are none', the saying would seem more absolute. But because he says: Thou shalt have none, he did not deny that there are, but forbade that they be gods to him to whom these precepts are given. From this I think Paul took: For although there be that are called gods, either in heaven or on earth etc. In other places also you will find them named, as there: "A great King above all gods", and: "The God of gods, the Lord". Of lords the same Apostle says: "Whether thrones, or dominations, etc." But dominations are nothing else than a certain order and multitude of lords. In which the Apostle seems to open the sense of the law, as if he should say: Though there be many lords, who rule over other nations, and many gods who are worshipped by others, yet to us there is one God, and one Lord. Whence, when the Most High divided the nations and scattered the sons of Adam, he appointed the bounds of the nations according to the number of the angels of God. The angels therefore, to whom the Most High committed the nations, Scripture calls lords or gods: gods, as given by God, and lords, as having received power by lot from the Lord. Whence it is said to them: "I have said: You are gods, and all of you the sons of the most High. But you like men shall die, and shall fall like one of the princes": imitating, namely, the devil, who was made prince of all to his ruin. Whence it is plain that transgression made them execrable, not nature. To thee therefore, O Israel, who art the portion of God and his lot, thou shalt have, he says, no other gods but me: because truly God is the one God, and truly the Lord is the one Lord; but on the others created by him he conferred this name not by nature, but by grace. These things are not said only to Israel according to the flesh, nay to you who have been made Israel by seeing God with the mind, and circumcised in heart, not in flesh. If yet you so act as to be worthy to be the portion of God, and to be measured in the lot of his inheritance; otherwise let them be an example to you who had been called to this, that they might be the portion of God, and, their sins requiring it, were scattered through all nations, and, brought out of the house of bondage, now serve not the Egyptians only, but all nations. For he who sins is the servant of sin.

04_marg1365: THOU SHALT NOT MAKE TO THYSELF A GRAVEN THING etc. ORIGEN. Thou shalt not make to thyself an idol, nor any likeness etc. Idols are one thing, gods another. For of gods the Apostle says: "For there be gods many, and lords many" etc. But of idols: "That an idol is nothing in the world." But of likenesses he did not add that they are nothing. But here it is said: Thou shalt not make to thyself an idol, nor the likeness of anything. It is one thing therefore to make an idol, another a likeness. For example: if anyone in gold and silver, wood or stone, makes the form of a four-footed beast, or a serpent, or a bird, and sets it up to be prayed to, he has made not an idol but a likeness. But he who makes what is not, namely a form which the eye has not seen, but the mind feigns for itself; as if anyone forms the head of a dog or a ram on human members, or two faces in the one figure of a man, or the hinder parts of a horse or fish to a human breast: he who does this makes not a likeness, but an idol. For he makes what is not, nor has anything like itself. Therefore the Apostle says: "that an idol is nothing in the world." For the form is not taken from any of the things that exist, but is what the idle and curious mind has found. But a likeness is when something is formed of the things that are either in heaven, or in earth, or in the waters; but not as it is easy to declare of the likenesses of the things that are on earth or in the sea, so too of the heavenly, where one may say this can be perceived of the sun and moon and stars, whose forms the gentiles express. But Moses, learned in all the wisdom of the Egyptians, desired to forbid even the things that were among them in secret, as Hecate, and other forms of demons, which the Apostle calls "the spirits of wickedness in the high places", of which perhaps it is said: "My sword is inebriated in heaven." For by these forms and likenesses they invoked demons to drive away or avoid evils. But it is to be known that when you have resolved to keep this commandment and to have only one God and Lord, this is to declare war on all the others, which you renounced in baptism, confessing God alone, Father and Son and Holy Ghost. But confessing this, unless we love the Lord our God with all our heart, cleaving to him with all our soul, with all our strength, we are not made the portion of the Lord, but, set on the border, we have those offended whom we flee, and do not make him propitious to whom we flee. To whom the prophet says: Woe to the double-minded. And again: How long do you halt on both feet? By those therefore we are beaten as runaways, and by our Lord we are not defended, as unstable. Whence: Thy lovers have become thy enemies. Many are the lovers of the soul, taken with her beauty, with whom she played the harlot, saying: I will go after my lovers, that give me my wine etc. These she offended by returning to her former husband. Unless therefore you abide with your husband in all faith, you are suspected for the crimes you have committed; he marks all your movements, looks and gait; he can bear to see in you nothing wanton any longer, nothing loose or prodigal. If therefore you neglect the grace received, and even entangle yourself in worldly business, straightway the unclean spirit returns with seven more wicked, that he may not be cast out again, and the last things become worse than the first. There is therefore no agreement of the temple of God with idols. If we are God's, we ought to be such that God dwells and walks in us. Whence: You that carry the vessels of the Lord, go out, and touch not the unclean thing: I will receive you etc. He says therefore: Thou shalt have no other gods but me.

04_marg1369: VISITING THE INIQUITY etc. ORIGEN. Rendering the sins of the fathers upon the children etc. The heretics say that this is not the word of a good God, who says that one is punished for the sins of another; yet they call the God of the law just. Nor can they show how he is just, if he punishes one when another sins. But our inner man is said either to have God for Father, if he lives according to God; or the devil, if he does his will. Whence: You are of your father the devil, and the desires of your father you will do. As therefore the seed of God is in us when, keeping the word of God, we do not sin, according to that: He who is of God sinneth not, because the seed of God abideth in him; so when we are persuaded by the devil to sin, we receive his seed; when we do what he persuades, he has now begotten us. For we are born his sons through sin. But because we scarcely sin without help, as no one commits adultery alone, but an adulteress must become partner, and, if not more, someone, man or woman, must be joined for the service of the crime: all these, begotten as it were one from another according to the order of persuasion, draw their lineage from the devil; as in the betrayal of the Lord the devil entered into the heart of Judas, and begot the first son of sin, who could not do this alone; he went therefore to the Scribes and Pharisees and the high priests. From Judas therefore is born the third and fourth generation of sin. Let us see therefore how God renders the sins of the fathers upon the children unto the third and fourth generation, and not upon the fathers themselves. For nothing is said of the fathers. The devil therefore, because he has now passed the measure of sinning, like a garment clotted with blood, will not be clean in this world, and is not scourged for sin: for all things are kept for him in the future. Whence: "Art thou come before the time to torment us?" But the sins are rendered upon the sons whom he begot through sin, who, set in the flesh, are scourged, because "God desireth not the death of the sinner, but rather that he be converted and live". Mercifully therefore he renders the sins of the fathers upon the children, because the devil and his angels, who are made the fathers even of sin, are unworthy to be corrected in the present: their sons, and those who through them have been taken into the fellowship of sin, receive in the present what they have done, that, being purged, they may not be made companions of the devil in punishment. Whence: "I will visit their iniquities with a rod." But my mercy I will not take away from them. For God is jealous, and does not wish the soul which he espouses to himself in faith to remain in the defilement of sin, but to be quickly purged. But if she will not be purged, he will laugh at their destruction, saying to them: "Depart from me, you cursed, into everlasting fire" etc. Let us know therefore that we are rebuked in the present, that in the future we may rest. Whence: When we are chastised, we are rebuked by the Lord, that we be not condemned with this world.

04_marg1375: Again it is wont to be asked whether fornication also is held under the name of mechia. For this is a Greek word, which Scripture now uses for the Latin. For in Greek it calls none moechi but adulterers. But the Law was given not to men only, but also to women. For let not the woman think nothing is commanded her here because it is said: Thou shalt not covet thy neighbour's wife, as though she might lawfully covet the husband of her neighbour. If therefore here, from what is said to the man: Thou shalt not covet thy neighbour's wife, what pertains to the woman also is understood, how much more by what is said: Thou shalt not commit adultery is each sex bound, since the precept itself can be referred to both, as "Thou shalt not kill", Thou shalt not steal, and the things which in like manner, no one sex being expressed, seem to sound to both; because the more honoured, that is, the male, is the one expressed. And hence a woman who has a husband is an adulteress by lying with one who is not her husband, even if he has no wife. A man also is an adulterer by lying with her who is not his wife, even if she has no husband. But whether, if a man who has no wife does it with a woman who has no husband, he is held by the transgression of this precept, is rightly asked. For if he is not held, fornication is not forbidden in the Decalogue, but only mechia, that is, adultery, although every adultery is fornication. Whence: Whosoever shall put away his wife, excepting the cause of fornication, maketh her to commit adultery. For here he called it fornication if she who has a husband sins with another, which is mechia, that is, adultery. But whether every fornication can be called mechia in the Scriptures, no example of the manner of speech occurs to me. But if not every fornication can be called mechia, where in the Decalogue that fornication is forbidden which men who have no wives commit with women who have no men or husbands, whether it can be found, I know not. But if by the name of theft every unlawful taking of another's thing is well understood (for he who forbade theft did not permit robbery, but wished the whole to be understood from the part, whatever is unlawfully taken of the things of one's neighbour), then by the name of mechia also every unlawful lying together, and the unlawful use of those members, ought to be understood as forbidden.

04_marg1388: Allegorically. It is to be known that, though the active and the contemplative life are both of the grace of God, the one is to us of necessity, the other of will. For no one knowing God enters into his kingdom unless he first works well. But they can enter without the contemplative who do not neglect the good things they can do. Hence it is said by Moses: If thou buy a Hebrew servant etc. Hebrew is interpreted 'passing over', and a Hebrew servant is bought when one who already passes over in mind from this world is made subject to the service of God. So Moses passed over that he might see the sight, and David says: "I passed by, and lo, he was not." This bought servant is commanded to serve six years, so that in the seventh he may go out free for nothing. For the number six signifies the perfection of the active life; the number seven, contemplation. He serves six years therefore, in the seventh he goes out free, because through the active life which he has perfectly shown forth he passes over to the freedom of the contemplative life. And it is to be noted that they go out free for nothing, because after they have done all things they say they are unprofitable servants; as the active life therefore was theirs by gift, so the contemplative will be of grace. With what raiment he came in, with the like let him go out: because it is needful that each one persevere in what he has begun until the end of the work, in the intention with which he began. For he passes over well to the contemplative who in the active did not change the raiment of his intention for the worse; and there are some who, after they are joined to the service of God, love to work. Others, after they have come to the service of God, learn to work well. He who first was zealous to have good works is the Hebrew servant bought with a wife, and for the most part he can pass over to the contemplative, yet not forsake the active life. Whence it is added: If having a wife, his wife also shall go out with him. For the wife goes out with him to freedom when he does not abandon the good action by which he may profit others. But if his master gave him a wife, and she hath borne sons and daughters: the woman and her children shall be her master's; but he himself shall go out with his raiment. The master gives a wife to the bought servant when the preacher joins to good action him whom he has given over to God. And preachers are called masters, as it is said to Eliseus of his preacher: Dost thou know that thy master will be taken from thee? The wife of the bought servant bears sons and daughters when good action brings forth for him strong and tender fruits. But the woman remains with her children to the master, and the servant goes out with his raiment, because good action and its fruit are reckoned to the preacher for reward. But he himself, persevering in the intention of desire, goes out by the grace of God to contemplation. And if the servant shall say: I love my master etc. The servant loves his master when he keeps the preacher's words with careful mind. Loving also his wife and children, he refuses to go out free, when, loving the active life and its fruits, he will not pass over to the contemplative; because, considering that he has the good works of his ministry in servitude, he refuses to pass over to the rest of freedom; but let his master bring him to the gods, and set him to the door and the posts, and bore his ear with an awl, that he may be a servant for ever. For he who has resolved to persevere in the active life is brought by the Lord to the gods when he is imbued by his preacher with the sayings of the ancient fathers, who have been priests to us in the way of God. He is led also to the door and posts of the tabernacle, both that he may hear something of the entrance of the eternal tabernacle, and may know finely the day of the dreadful judgment, lest by the good works he does he seek to please men. And so his ear is bored with an awl, that is, the mind with the fineness of the fear of God, that, pierced by the point of the word, in all that he does he may know how to attend to the entrance of the kingdom, and bear as it were an ear bored at the door and post of the tabernacle. And he shall be a servant for ever, that after the world he may be free: "Because the creature also itself shall be delivered from the servitude of corruption, into the liberty of the glory of the children of God." For then shall there be true liberty for us, when our adoption has come to the glory of the children of God. But now not only is the active life in servitude, but contemplation itself, by which we are rapt above ourselves, does not perfectly obtain the freedom of the mind, but imitates it, because that inmost rest is seen in a dark manner.
04_marg1389: SIX YEARS etc. ISIDORE. Allegorically. But if we have not willed it, the ear will be bored in witness of disobedience, and with our wife and children, whom we preferred to freedom, that is, with the flesh and its works, we shall serve sin for ever.

But if he take another for him, he shall not defraud her of the things that are needful, and her raiment, and her converse. But if he do not these three things to her, she shall go out free without price. They have made a most obscure place of an unusual manner of speech. But I will open it as I can. If any man sell his daughter to be a servant, that is, that she be a household servant (whom the Greeks call oiketen), she shall not go away as bondwomen depart. It is to be understood: She shall not depart in the way that Hebrew bondwomen depart after six years. For the law kept in the males must be understood as given also for the Hebrew woman. Why then shall she not depart so, unless because she is understood to have been so humbled in her service that her master has joined himself with her? Whence it follows: But if she please not her master, because he has now not named her, that is, has not made her his wife, he shall reward her; this is what he said above: She shall not go away as bondwomen depart. For she is bidden to receive something, because she has been humbled, because he did not so join himself with her as to make her his wife, that is, to name her to himself. But to a foreign nation he is not master to sell her, since he has despised her; that is, not because he has despised her is he therefore master to sell her; that is, he is not so much master that he may lawfully sell her to a foreign nation. 'He has despised in her' is the same as 'he has despised her'. And he despised her, that is, humbled her by lying with her and not making her his wife. But if the son has named her, he shall do to her according to the justification of daughters; that is: if he has joined her as wife to his son, he shall give her a dowry as to a daughter. But if he take another for him, that is, has not assigned this one as wife to his son, he shall not defraud her of the things that are needful, and her raiment, and her converse, since she did not remain wife to his son, in the manner he would give if he had not named her to himself. But where we have said: he shall not defraud her converse, the Greek has homilian, that is, speech, so calling lying together more modestly; that is, he shall give a reward for the lying together. So also Daniel, signifying lying together, says: "Under what tree didst thou see them conferring together?" And elsewhere: "Then they that feared spoke to you." But if he do not these three things to her, she shall go out free; that is: if he has neither humbled her himself by lying with her, nor joined her to his son, nor cast her out when another was taken by the son. She shall go away free, that is, it will suffice her not to be held in servitude. She shall go away receiving nothing, as the Hebrew servant. For it will not be lawful for the master to couple her to a man not a Hebrew, since it is not lawful for her to be handed to a foreign nation. But if he has coupled her to a Hebrew servant, it is understood that she will go out with him free, not separated from her husband.
