04_marg1392: BUT HE THAT DID NOT etc. RABANUS. For homicides not done willingly six cities of refuge are appointed: Cedes in Galilee, of mount Nephthali, and Sichem in mount Ephraim, and Cariatharbe, which is Hebron, in mount Juda; and beyond the Jordan, over against Jericho toward the east, Bosor, which is in the plain of the wilderness, of the tribe of Ruben, and Ramoth in Galaad, of the tribe of Gad, and Gaulon in Basan, of the tribe of Manasses. These were appointed for the children of Israel and the strangers, that they might not die, even at the hand of the neighbour desiring to avenge the blood shed, until he set forth his cause before the people. Mystically: if anyone through lying in wait or hatred has struck another with the sword of malice, and seduced him into the death of the soul, he himself will be liable to eternal death. Whence: He that shall scandalize one of these little ones that believe in me, it were better for him etc. And: Whosoever hateth his brother is a murderer. And we know that no murderer hath eternal life. This one is commanded to be taken from the altar of the Lord, because, being unworthy of the Lord's sacraments, he is deservedly removed from communion. But he who has hurt someone through carelessness or ignorance has a city of refuge, namely the catholic Church, where, repenting, he may be zealous in good works through all the time of the present life; and if he has set his hope in the death of the high priest, that is, Christ, he will be saved.
04_marg1393: But if unwillingly, but God delivered him into his hands etc. This is said as if, even though not willing to kill, he could kill, where God delivered him into his hands. It is understood therefore that God alone did it, and for this alone, because God did it, it is said: but God delivered him into his hands. But when he kills willingly, both he himself kills and God delivered him into his hands. This therefore is the difference: that there God alone did it; but here both God and man, because of the will of the doer. But not as God, so man. For God did it justly, but man is worthy of punishment: not because he killed him whom God did not will to be killed, but because he did it through iniquity. For he did not lend his ministry to God commanding, but served the lust of his own malice. In the same deed therefore God is praised for his hidden equity, and man is punished for his own iniquity. For not because God "spared not even his own Son, but delivered him up for us all" did Judas therefore justly deliver him.

04_marg1397: Since he would not have the unformed offspring pertain to homicide, he certainly did not reckon it a man. Here there is a question about the soul: whether what is not formed cannot be understood to be even ensouled, and therefore it is not homicide, because it cannot be said to be deprived of life if it does not yet have a soul. For he follows and says: But if it was formed, he shall give life for life, that is, he shall die. According to that: "Eye for eye", and "tooth for tooth", and the like, namely by the equity of retaliation, which the Law established for this reason, to show what vengeance is due. For otherwise it would not be known what pardon remits, so that it might be said: "Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors." Debtors therefore are shown by the Law, that when there is forgiving, it may appear what is remitted: for otherwise we would not remit. If therefore that unformed offspring already was, but still in some manner formlessly ensouled, since the great question of the soul is not to be rushed, the Law therefore would not have it pertain to homicide, because it cannot yet be called a living soul in a body which lacks sense, if such it is in flesh not yet formed, and therefore not yet endowed with senses.
04_marg1398: But if two men strive, and strike a woman with child, and her infant come forth not yet formed, he shall suffer loss, as much as the husband of the woman shall lay upon him, and shall give for his soul. But if it was formed, he shall give life for life, eye for eye etc. First let us see of that which came forth not yet formed, how one of those striving is commanded to be struck with the loss of money, when two are spoken of. What too of this, that the husband of the woman lays it 'on him', and not 'on them'; and 'he shall give', and not rather 'they shall give'? But if the infant came forth already formed, we easily understand giving life for life: namely that the sin be avenged by death. But what follows it is worth the pains to unfold. For it does not seem that even a formed infant, struck by the heel of one striving, lost an eye in the womb; and teeth it had none at all. For if we refer this to the mother, how does the miscarrying woman lose an eye, or suffer in her teeth? But grant that she miscarried being struck either in the eye or in the tooth, and received a stripe or a wound; what do we say also of burning for burning? Could the woman standing by the striving men be burned, that burning should be paid for burning? In Deuteronomy also these things cannot easily be unfolded. Yet in the Scriptures the members of the soul are named by the same words and offices with which the members of the body are used or called. Whence: Thou seest the mote in thy brother's eye, and the beam that is in thy own eye thou seest not. And elsewhere: "He that hath ears to hear, let him hear." And: "How beautiful are the feet of them that preach the gospel of peace." Let not the likeness of the words therefore trouble us. There are therefore two striving, two disputing about doctrines or questions of the law, and quarrelling over battles of words. Whence the Apostle: Contend not in words etc. And elsewhere: Avoid questions of the law, knowing that they beget strifes. Because therefore these strive in a question "to the subverting of the hearers", they strike a woman with child, and cast out the infant formed, or still unformed. The woman with child is the name for the soul which has newly conceived the word of God. Whence: From thy fear, O Lord, we have conceived in the womb and brought forth. They therefore who conceive and at once bring forth are to be counted not women, but men, and perfect. Whence: If the earth hath brought forth in one day, and a nation is born together in one day. This then is the generation of the perfect, which is conceived and born on the same day. And men bring forth according to that: "My little children, of whom I am in labour again, until Christ be formed in you." The perfect therefore and men bring forth at once, that is, they bring the word of faith conceived to works. But the soul which conceives and keeps in the womb and does not bring forth is called a woman. Whence: The pains of childbirth have come upon her, and there is not strength to bring forth in her. This one therefore, when two strive among themselves and bring forth scandals, is struck and scandalized, so that she casts away the word of faith which she had faintly conceived, not yet formed. For in some the word is formed, in some not formed. Whence: "Until Christ be formed in you." For Christ is the Word of God. He therefore who struck it out shall suffer loss. Of the losses of doctors therefore the Apostle says: If any man's work burn, he shall suffer loss etc. And the Lord himself in the Gospel: What doth it profit a man, if he gain the whole world, and lose his own soul? Whence it seems to be shown that certain sins pertain to loss, yet not to destruction, because he who has suffered loss is said to be saved, though by fire. Whence John says that certain sins are unto death. But which are unto death, which not unto death, cannot easily be discerned: for "who can understand sins?" But when it is related that on five pounds other five were gained, and on two, two, he who loses the reward of this gain is said to be struck with loss, as he who gave a cause of scandal to the weaker and womanly soul. And he shall give according as her husband shall lay upon him, and he shall give with honour to the soul of the learner. The husband is the master, Christ, or he who for Christ is the doctor of souls. He therefore shall suffer loss who contends "to the subverting of the hearers", for the soul which did not yet have a formed infant; which can be taken of the scandal of a catechumen. It can also be that he who hurt her may instruct and restore to the soul what she lost, and with honour and modesty, namely with meekness, not with strife, as when he brought the scandal. But when it was formed, he shall give life for life. The formed infant can be seen as the word of God in the heart of the soul which has received the grace of baptism, or which has received the word of God more evidently and clearly. He therefore who struck shall render life for life at the day of judgment, namely before that judge who can destroy both soul and body in hell. As one who is conscious to himself of so great a scandal, let him lay down his soul for the soul of the one scandalized, and give his labour even unto death how she may be restored to the faith. Let him lay down eye for eye: if he hurt the eye of the soul, that is, troubled its understanding, let his eye be taken away from him who is over the Church, that is, his understanding. If he hurt the tooth, which, receiving the food of the word of God, was wont to break it small or grind it with the grinders, that it might send on a fine sense to the belly of the soul; if he has troubled and pulled out this tooth, so that by its grinding the soul cannot receive the word of God finely and spiritually, his tooth shall be taken away who does not break small and divide well the foods of the word. For this perhaps it is said of the Lord: "Thou hast broken the teeth of sinners." And elsewhere: "The Lord shall break the grinders of the lions." So therefore the soul is said to be hurt and struck through its members. He demands also hand for hand, and foot for foot. The hand is the power of the soul by which it can hold and grasp something, as its act and strength; and the foot that by which it walks to good or to evil. Because therefore the scandalized soul is cast down not only in faith but also in acts, which are signified by the hands, his hands are taken away with which he does not work well, and the feet with which he does not walk well. He will receive also burning, because he burned the soul and delivered it to hell. Through each of these it is shown that the striker, all his members cut off, is to be cut off from the body of the Church, that the rest seeing it may have fear and not do the like. Therefore the Apostle, when he describes the doctor of the Church, among other things commands "no striker", lest, striking women with child, that is, beginning souls, he should lay down life for life, eye for eye, tooth for tooth etc. Of such it is said: "Woe to them that are with child, and that give suck in those days", in which even the elect are scandalized, if it can be. Yet it is to be known that it is not for the perfect to be scandalized, but for women or little ones. Whence: If anyone shall scandalize one of these little ones etc.

Or according to that of the Apostle: For although there be that are called gods, either in heaven or on earth, as there are gods many and lords many; for by adding 'as there are', he wished those to be understood as gods who are even worthily so called, to whom however latria, that is, the service which pertains to religion, is not due, but to the one true God, who is God to us? But these are forbidden to be cursed, not commanded to be honoured with sacrifices or any services of latria.
04_marg1416: ISIDORE. By the firstfruits of the crops or of the firstborn are shown the first beginnings of good works, or the good will, which is prior to the work, which the Pelagians offend by attributing it to themselves. But God, when he commands it to be offered to him by us, shows that it pertains to his grace. But in the tithes the number ten signifies perfection, because number grows up to it. And therefore, as in the firstfruits the beginnings of our wills, so in the tithes we are commanded to refer the completions of our works to God, by whom both the beginning of good work and the effect of perfection are given.

04_marg1419: SIX YEARS THOU SHALT SOW etc. AUGUSTINE. It is asked what the poor gather, if in the seventh year the land is so spared that it is not even sown. For what is said: The poor of thy nation shall eat, does not pertain to the vineyard and the oliveyard, because from unsown land they can take nothing, where crops cannot spring. For of the vineyard and the oliveyard he says afterward that the like is to be done. Therefore that is understood of the tilled fields, which serve for corn. Or is it to be taken thus: Six years thou shalt sow thy land, and shalt gather; but the seventh thou shalt not gather; so that 'thou shalt sow' is understood even though it is not said, so that sowing and gathering pertain to the six years, but to the seventh, letting alone what was sown? For what will the poor have from it, whose leavings he gave even to the wild beasts, namely to those which can feed on those crops, that is, boars, stags, and such like? Which yet would not be said, except for the sake of signification. For God has no care for oxen. Which is not so understood as if he does not feed those which "neither sow, nor reap", but because it is no care of his to move man by a precept how he should look to his ox: how much less then is it his care to give precepts about wild beasts, since he himself feeds them with the riches of nature, who feeds them also through the other six years, when the things sown are gathered?
04_marg1420: SIX YEARS THOU SHALT SOW THY GROUND etc. In the number six the perfection of works is expressed, in the number seven the rest of souls. Well therefore are we commanded to sow our land six years and gather its crops, because in the present life, which consists of six ages, we ought to till the land of our flesh and sow in it the seeds of the virtues, that in the future we may receive eternal life. And that the poor of the people and the beasts of the field are commanded to eat what grows in the seventh year from our past labour signifies that through the service of almsgiving and charity a reward is prepared in the future. Which the vineyard and the oliveyard also, that is, the works of grace and mercy, prepare. If therefore we are beneficent not only to friends but also to beasts, that is, to enemies, in the future, when there will no longer be time for working, we shall obtain rewards. Whence: "He who soweth in blessings shall also reap of blessings" eternal life.

04_marg1427: THOU SHALT NOT BOIL A KID etc. AUGUSTINE. How it is to be understood according to the proper sense of the words I know not whether it can be found. For if we take it that a lamb is forbidden to be boiled in milk for the sake of some signification, there is no custom of boiling so. But if in the days when it is suckled, which of the Jews ever kept this, not to boil a lamb unless it had ceased to suck? And what is in the milk of his dam, as if, even if this were understood, it could be boiled without transgression of this precept if, its mother having died when it was born, it were suckled by another ewe? That the precept is for the sake of some signification, therefore, no one doubts. But even the things that can be done in observance were not commanded so without cause. For they signify something: but how this is to be observed according to the proper sense of the words either does not exist or does not appear. Yet I approve the understanding of it concerning Christ, who was foretold by this prophecy not to be killed by the Jews as an infant, when Herod, seeking to kill him, did not find him; so that 'thou shalt boil', which is said, pertains to the fire of the passion, that is, tribulation. That too perhaps is not absurd which others say, that this was commanded by way of prophecy, that the good Israelites should not join themselves to the wicked Jews, by whom Christ suffered as a lamb in the milk of his mother, that is, at that time in which he was conceived. For women are said to gather milk from the time they conceive: but Christ was born, the ninth month completed and the tenth begun, on the eighth of the kalends of January, and was conceived in the first month, namely on the eighth of the kalends of April, which was also the time of his passion, in the milk of his mother, that is, on the day on which he was conceived. Or: upon those still little and sucking thou shalt not bring the passion; as if it were said to Christ, who spared such disciples still. Whence: "If therefore you seek me, let these go their way." Whence the Evangelist adds: "That the word might be fulfilled which he said: Of them whom thou hast given me, I have not lost any one." Whence it appears that they, if they had suffered then, would have perished; but afterward they suffered, not as lambs in milk, but as rams in the flock.

04_marg1430: I WILL BE AN ENEMY etc. GREGORY. The root of all evil is pride, of which it is said: Pride is the beginning of all sin. Its first offspring are the seven principal vices: vainglory, envy, anger, sadness, avarice, gluttony, lust. And because our Redeemer grieved that we were taken captive by these seven vices of pride, he came full of the Spirit of sevenfold grace to the spiritual battle of deliverance.
04_marg1431: AND MY ANGEL SHALL GO BEFORE THEE etc. RABANUS. Josue brought the Israelite people into the land of promise, casting out seven nations, and destroying their idols and altars. Mystically, the true God exterminates these nations with their images when he expels from our hearts the seven principal vices and every idol of the enemy, that we may securely possess the land of our nature.
04_marg1432: JOHN CHRYSOSTOM. Each vice has in our heart its own dwelling, which claiming for itself, in the recess of our soul it exterminates Israel, that is, the contemplation of the highest things, and does not cease to oppose. For virtues cannot dwell with vices; but when the vices have been overcome by the Israelites, that is, by the virtues, the place which the spirit of concupiscence or fornication possessed, chastity will hold. That which fury had seized, patience will claim. That which sadness working death had occupied, saving gladness full of joy will possess. That which sloth laid waste, fortitude will till. That which pride trod down, humility will honour. And so, each vice being expelled, their places, that is, their dispositions, the contrary virtues will possess, which are called the children of Israel, that is, souls seeing God; who, when they have expelled all the passions of the heart, are to be believed not so much to have gained others' possessions as to have recovered their own; because, according to the old tradition, the sons of Sem received by lot the land of the Chanaanites in the division of the world, which the Chanaanites possessed by violence. Whence by the just judgment of God they were driven out. The will of the Lord also assigned the possession of our heart not to vices but to virtues, which, after the transgression of Adam, when the vices grew insolent, as the Chanaanites, were driven from their own region. But when through the grace of God they are restored by our diligence and our labour, they do not so much occupy another's land as receive back their own.

04_marg1434: SENDING OUT HORNETS etc. AUGUSTINE. I will send wasps etc. God promises this, and the book of Wisdom says it was fulfilled, where it says: He sent wasps, forerunners of his host. But we do not read that it was done either in the time of Moses, or under Josue, or under the judges, or under the kings. Therefore perhaps the wasps are to be understood as the stings of fear by which the nations were harried, that they might give way to the children of Israel. For God speaks, in whose speech, if something is said figuratively which was not fulfilled according to the proper sense, it does not hinder the faith of the history, in which the truthfulness of the narrator is seen; as neither is the narrative of the Evangelists hindered according to the proper sense if something is said figuratively by Christ.

For when the saints fight against the greater vices and conquer, they leave the lesser, and these are permitted to rule, lest through elation they fall more grievously. Whence a sting of the flesh was given to Paul for the guarding of humility.
